It is a symbol of Cambodia and appears on the Cambodian national flag.
Overfishing in the flooded forest around the Tonle Sap Lake is a major threat to D. pulcher
siamese-tiger-perch.notes: Confirmed all four quotes on the cited pages. "Fed" is a fair paraphrase of the lake district as a fishing and farming area that maintained Angkor. Tonle Sap is in the input range and Amazonas confirms a native Tonle Sap form of D. pulcher.

patagonian-seahorse.clue: Its coast runs from the cattle country of horseback gauchos south into a windy land that early explorers thought was home to giants.
evidence: It inhabits coastal waters from northeastern Brazil to Chubut, Argentina.
Southwest Atlantic: Brazil (south), Uruguay and Argentina.
The figure of the gaucho is a folk symbol mainly in Argentina and Uruguay
was a migratory horseman, and adept in cattle work
the extent of Patagonia could be defined as the provinces of Neuquén, Río Negro, Chubut and Santa Cruz
Magellan used this term in 1520 to describe the native tribes of the region, whom his expedition thought to be giants.
Patagonia's notorious winds have already made the area Argentina's main source of wind power
patagonian-seahorse.notes: All claims confirmed. The "notorious winds" sentence is in the second half of the Patagonia article. The range ends at Chubut, which is a Patagonian province, so "south into" Patagonia is accurate. The clue points to the Atlantic coast of Uruguay and Argentina, which is in range.

halmahera-walking-shark.clue: Its reefs lie in the spice islands, once the only place on earth cloves were found, where sultans grew rich as the world's major clove producer.
evidence: This species is described from two specimens collected near Ternate island in 2013, off the coast of larger Halmahera island.
Halmahera, formerly known as Jilolo, Gilolo, or Jailolo, is the largest island in the Maluku Islands.
The islands were known as the Spice Islands because of the nutmeg, mace, and cloves that were exclusively found there
Ternate and Tidore were the world's major producer of cloves, from which their rulers became among the wealthiest and most powerful sultans in the Indonesian region.
It is off the west coast of Halmahera
halmahera-walking-shark.notes: Original: "Its reefs ring the original spice islands, whose sultans grew rich as the world's main source of cloves." The sources support neither "original" nor "main source" (they say "major producer"), and "ring" overstated a range limited to Halmahera. Changed it to "lie in the spice islands, once the only place on earth cloves were found, where sultans grew rich as the world's major clove producer". The "only place" wording also steers players away from the clove-growing sultanate of Zanzibar.

golden-cave-catfish.clue: Its cave lies in a dry country named after what is called the world's oldest desert, home to the highest sand dunes on earth.
evidence: This cavefish is only known to live in the Aigamas cave, Otjozondjupa region, Namibia.
Namibia is the driest country in sub-Saharan Africa.
The name of the country is derived from the Namib desert, the oldest desert in the world.
Its sand dunes, created by the strong onshore winds, are the highest in the world.
golden-cave-catfish.notes: Original began "Its underground lake lies...". No cited source mentions a lake, and the funFact already uses "its underground lake", so I changed it to "Its cave lies". The Namibia article supports the rest word for word, including "driest country in sub-Saharan Africa" for "dry".

fiery-redfin.clue: Its streams run through the only region on earth where rooibos tea is farmed, about 250 km north of a city beneath a flat-topped mountain.
evidence: The fish is endemic to South Africa, where it can be found in the Oudste, Thee, Noordhoeks, Boskloof and Rondegat tributaries of the Olifants River system on the western side of the Cederberg Mountains
Rooibos is farmed exclusively in a 60,000 ha (150,000 acres) area in the Cederberg region of South Africa, some 155 mi (249 km) north of Cape Town.
is a flat-topped mountain forming a prominent landmark overlooking the city of Cape Town
fiery-redfin.notes: Rooibos is farmed "exclusively" in the Cederberg, about 249 km north of Cape Town, and the fish lives only in western Cederberg tributaries. Table Mountain overlooks Cape Town. All quotes confirmed.

somali-cavefish.clue: It lives underground in a dry country at the very tip of its continent's horn-shaped point, a land with more camels than anywhere else on earth.
evidence: endemic to Somalia
A blind species which inhabits underground waters in Somalia
conditions in Somalia range from arid in the northeastern and central regions to semiarid in the northwest and south
the country occupies the tip of a region that, due to its resemblance on the map to a rhinoceros' horn, is commonly referred to as the Horn of Africa.
Somalia has the largest population of camels in the world.
somali-cavefish.notes: Original began "Its wells lie in a dry country...". The cited sources don't mention wells (FishBase says "underground waters"), and wells echo the revealFact, so I changed it to "It lives underground in a dry country". I confirmed "dry" from the climate section: central Somalia, where Bud Bud is, is arid.

cave-angelfish.clue: Its caves lie in the misty, most mountainous province of the only country in its region never colonised by a western power.
evidence: The species has been recorded from eight subterranean sites within a large karst system (Pang Mapha karst formation) in Mae Hong Son Province, Thailand.
It is hemmed in by the high mountain ranges of the Shan Hills and is the most mountainous province in Thailand
The province is often covered with mist.
Thailand remains the only Southeast Asian state never colonised by a Western power
cave-angelfish.notes: All quotes confirmed. The "never colonised" sentence is in the second half of the Thailand article; the lead also says Siam "remained the only country in Southeast Asia to avoid colonisation by European powers".

mccullochs-anemonefish.clue: Its island has the world's southernmost barrier coral reef and lies 600 km off the east coast of the world's smallest continent.
evidence: Southwest Pacific: Lord Howe Island.
the world's southernmost barrier coral reef
It lies 600 km (370 mi; 320 nmi) directly east of mainland Port Macquarie
The mainland is the world's smallest continent
mccullochs-anemonefish.notes: Confirmed on Lord Howe Island, FishBase and Australia pages. Lord Howe is the core of the input range. Wikipedia's mention of Norfolk Island is not used.

red-stumpnose.clue: Its range begins in a bay lined with suburbs of a city beneath a flat-topped mountain, where penguins stroll along a popular beach.
evidence: between False Bay and East London
Suburbs of Cape Town stretch right across the Cape Flats, from Simon's Town halfway down the Cape Peninsula
is a flat-topped mountain forming a prominent landmark overlooking the city of Cape Town
The beach is a popular tourist spot because of a colony of the endemic and critically endangered African penguins
It is located on the eastern side of the Cape Peninsula, in Simon's Town, in the southern region of Cape Town, South Africa.
the clear water of False Bay
red-stumpnose.notes: The range runs from False Bay east to East London, so "begins" in that bay is accurate. Boulders Beach is on False Bay in Simon's Town, and its penguin colony makes it a popular tourist spot.

magnificent-pearlfish.clue: It lives in the basin of the longest river that flows entirely within its country, which is the world's fifth-largest country by area.
evidence: South America: Middle São Francisco River basin, Brazil.
it is the longest river that runs entirely in Brazilian territory
It is also the world's fifth-largest country by area and the seventh-largest by population, with over 214 million people.
magnificent-pearlfish.notes: Original ended "which is the biggest country on its continent". That never says which continent, and "longest river entirely within one country" is the Yangtze's famous record, so it could send players to China. I changed it to "which is the world's fifth-largest country by area", taken word for word from the Brazil article.

doubleheader-wrasse.clue: One of its islands was once a prison for the worst convicts, later settled by descendants of a famous ship's mutineers.
evidence: Southwest Pacific: Australia, Lord Howe Island, Middleton Reef, and Norfolk Island.
Lord Howe Island, Norfolk Island, Middleton Reef, and more rarely, New South Wales.
The island served as a convict penal settlement from 6 March 1788 until 5 May 1855
as a place to send "the worst description of convicts."
On 8 June 1856, permanent civilian residence on the island began when descendants of the Bounty mutineers
descendants of the Bounty mutineers were relocated from Pitcairn Island
doubleheader-wrasse.notes: Original said "a harsh convict prison". The Norfolk Island article never calls the settlement harsh, so I changed it to "a prison for the worst convicts", from the 1824 order to send "the worst description of convicts". Rated hard: placing it needs the Pitcairn-to-Norfolk move, and players who link the mutineers only to Pitcairn may pin the wrong island.

blackfin-icefish.clue: Its icy waters surround the mountainous island a famous polar explorer crossed on foot to get help for his stranded crew, and where he now lies buried.
evidence: with the type locality given as South Georgia Island
Most research on the blackfin icefish has been carried out around the Scotia Arc, encompassing South Georgia,

After making a foot crossing of the island with Tom Crean and Frank Worsley, Ernest Shackleton organised the rescue of his party from Elephant Island following the disaster that befell the 1916 Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition, which he led.
He is buried in the cemetery at Grytviken alongside Frank Wild.
The terrain is mountainous, with a central ridge and many fjords and bays along the coast.
blackfin-icefish.notes: All quotes confirmed. South Georgia is the type locality and is in the input range. I chose this over the Scotia Arc clue (also accurate and medium) because the Shackleton story is more fun and points at one island in the range.

maltese-skate.clue: It lives in the narrow channel between a big island and the coast of the ancient city whose general marched war elephants over the mountains.
evidence: now appears to be restricted to the Sicilian channel
All ships crossing the sea had to pass between Sicily and the coast of Tunisia
was a Carthaginian general and statesman who commanded the forces of Carthage
Hannibal invaded Italy by crossing the Alps with North African war elephants.
The Strait of Sicily (also known as Sicilian Strait, Sicilian Channel, Channel of Sicily, Sicilian Narrows,
both the largest and most populous island in the Mediterranean Sea
maltese-skate.notes: Wording unchanged. The researcher's sources didn't support "narrow" or "big island", so I added the Strait of Sicily article ("Sicilian Narrows") and the Sicily article (largest island in the Mediterranean). Carthage stood on the Tunisian coast of that channel, and Hannibal crossed the Alps with war elephants.

mangarahara-cichlid.clue: Its river is on the world's fourth-largest island, sometimes called the 'eighth continent', and the world's principal supplier of vanilla.
evidence: endemic to certain river systems in northern Madagascar
it is the world's fourth-largest island
This distinctive ecology has led some ecologists to refer to Madagascar as the "eighth continent"
Madagascar is the world's principal supplier of vanilla, cloves, and ylang-ylang.
mangarahara-cichlid.notes: Original ended "whose top export is vanilla", but the source gives only 2017 export figures ("In 2017 the top exports were vanilla..."), so the present tense overstated it. I replaced it with "and the world's principal supplier of vanilla", which the Madagascar article states directly.

denisons-barb.clue: Its hill streams are in the first state of its country to be soaked by the monsoon each year, a state famous for houseboats on its backwaters.
evidence: endemic to the fast-flowing hill streams and rivers of the Western Ghats in India
Denison barb is endemic to the Achankovil, Pamba and Chaliyar rivers.
Though the Government of Kerala banned the fishing and export of the endangered barb
making Kerala the first state in India to receive rain from the Southwest monsoon.
Kettuvallam (Kerala houseboats) in the backwaters are one of the prominent tourist attractions in Kerala.
denisons-barb.notes: All quotes confirmed. "Famous for houseboats" is a fair paraphrase of "one of the prominent tourist attractions". The Achankovil, Pamba and Chaliyar are Kerala rivers in the input range.

sulphur-limia.clue: Its spring sits on the shore of a salty lake 46 m below sea level, home to crocodiles and rhinoceros iguanas, on an island split between two countries.
evidence: Only known from the sulfur spring at Balneario La Zurza on the Dominican Republic's southeastern shore of Lake Enriquillo.
Lake Enriquillo (Spanish: Lago Enriquillo) is a hypersaline lake in the Dominican Republic located in the southwestern region of the country.
Lake Enriquillo covers an area of 380 km2 (150 sq mi), and is the lowest point for an island country, falling 46 m (151 ft) below sea level.
Lake Enriquillo is home to the largest population of American crocodiles (Crocodylus acutus) in the Caribbean.
Two endangered iguanas endemic to Hispaniola live sympatrically on around the lake, as well as on Isla Cabritos: the Ricord's iguana (Cyclura ricordii), and the rhinoceros iguana (Cyclura cornuta).

Covering an area of 76,192-square-kilometre (29,418 sq mi), it is divided into two separate sovereign countries: the Spanish–speaking Dominican Republic (48,445 km2 (18,705 sq mi)) to the east and the French and Haitian Creole–speaking Haiti (27,750 km2 (10,710 sq mi)) to the west.
sulphur-limia.notes: All quotes found verbatim on the current pages. They support every claim: a hypersaline lake 46 m below sea level, with crocodiles and rhinoceros iguanas, on an island split between two countries. The spring on its south-eastern shore is the fish's only known site.

sawbwa-barb.clue: Its lake is famous for fishermen who row standing on one leg, gliding past stilt houses and vegetable gardens that float on the water.
evidence: The species is endemic to Inle Lake in Myanmar (Burma).
Local fishermen are known for practicing a distinctive rowing style which involves standing at the stern on one leg and wrapping the other leg around the oar.
Almost all the houses in the village on the lake itself sit on stilts and are made of woven bamboo.
In addition to fishing, locals grow vegetables and fruit in large gardens that float on the surface of the lake.
sawbwa-barb.notes: Leg-rowing, stilt houses and floating vegetable gardens are all on the Inle Lake page, and the fish is endemic to that lake. I swapped the researcher's generic stilt-house quote for one that places the houses on the lake itself.

clipperton-angelfish.clue: Its only home is an uninhabited coral ring about 1,300 km off a resort city known for its cliff divers, yet it belongs to a country far across the world.
evidence: It is endemic to Clipperton Island, a French possession in the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Clipperton Island (French: La Passion–Clipperton [la pasjɔ̃ klipœʁtɔn]; Spanish: Isla de la Pasión), also known as Clipperton Atoll and previously as Clipperton's Rock, is an 8.9 km2 (3.4 sq mi) uninhabited coral atoll in the eastern Pacific Ocean.

The only French territory in the North Pacific, Clipperton is 10,675 km (5,764 nmi) from Paris, France; 5,400 km (2,900 nmi) from Papeete, French Polynesia; and 1,280 km (690 nmi) from Acapulco, Guerrero.
Clipperton is a ring-shaped atoll that completely encloses a stagnant fresh water lagoon and measures 12 km (7.5 mi) in circumference and 720 hectares (2.8 sq mi) in area.
Acapulco is also Mexico's largest beach and balneario resort city.
Anchored by attractions such as the beaches of Caleta and Caletilla, the cliff divers of La Quebrada, and the city square, known as El Zocalo.
Another attraction at Acapulco is the La Quebrada Cliff Divers.
clipperton-angelfish.notes: Changed 'on the far side of the world' to 'far across the world': France is about 10,700 km away, which is far but not the opposite side of the globe. Also changed 'famous for cliff divers' to 'known for its cliff divers', because the source calls them an attraction, not famous. 'Uninhabited' now cites the article's opening sentence rather than 'mostly uninhabited'.

pindu.clue: Its crater lake lies in a country nicknamed its continent 'in miniature', on the same volcano chain as a lake that burst out a huge cloud of gas in 1986.
evidence: It is endemic to Lake Barombi Mbo, a volcanic crater lake with a diameter of just 3 miles in western Cameroon where only the top 40 metres contains acceptable oxygen levels to harbor vertebrate life.
It is located in the Cameroon volcanic chain, and is the largest volcanic lake in this region.
Tourist literature describes Cameroon as "Africa in miniature" because it exhibits all major climates and vegetation of the continent: coast, desert, mountains, rainforest, and savanna.
The mountain is part of the area of volcanic activity known as the Cameroon Volcanic Line, which also includes Lake Nyos, the site of a disaster in 1986.
In 1986, Lake Nyos, a crater lake in the Oku volcanic plain, released a cloud of carbon dioxide gas that killed at least 1,200 people.
On 21 August 1986, one of these, Lake Nyos, belched carbon dioxide and killed between 1,700 and 2,000 people.
pindu.notes: Every quote is present. The two pages give different tolls (at least 1,200, or 1,700-2,000), so 'over 1,000' is safe. Both lakes sit on the same volcanic line, and 'Africa in miniature' is quoted directly. Lead edit: dropped the death toll to keep clues cheerful; the 1986 gas release is still supported by the cited evidence.

red-tailed-silverside.clue: Its river meets the sea on the east coast of the world's fourth-largest island, at a town that a cyclone left 90% destroyed in 2022.
evidence: The red-tailed silverside, or zona (Bedotia geayi) is a species of Madagascar rainbowfish endemic to the Mananjary River drainage in Madagascar.
It drains to the eastern coast, into the Indian Ocean.
Its mouth is situated in the city of Mananjary.
Mananjary is a city on the East coast of Madagascar with a population of 25,222 inhabitants in 2018.
In 2022 Cyclone Batsirai made landfall at Mananjary, leaving the city 90% destroyed.
Lying off the southeastern coast of Africa, it is the world's fourth-largest island, the second-largest island country, and the 46th-largest country overall.
red-tailed-silverside.notes: The river's mouth is at Mananjary on the east coast, the 2022 cyclone and 90% figure are quoted directly, and the island is the fourth-largest. I chose this over the lemur clue because it is medium rather than easy.

marojejy-bedotia.clue: Its streams tumble from rainforest mountains in the region that grows more vanilla than anywhere else on earth, on a huge island famous for lemurs.
evidence: This species was described by Melanie Stiassny nd Ian Harrison in 2000 from types collected from the Manantenina River on the south eastern boundary of the Marojejy National Park, after which the species is named.
Marojejy National Park () is a national park in the Sava region of northeastern Madagascar.
It covers 55,500 ha (214 sq mi) and is centered on the Marojejy Massif, a mountain chain that rises to an elevation of 2,132 m (6,995 ft).

Warm, dense rainforest can be found at lower elevations, followed by shorter forests at higher elevations, followed still by cloud forest, and topped near the peaks with the only remaining undisturbed mountain scrub in Madagascar.
Each of these towns claims itself the World Capital of Vanilla, a spice of which the region is the largest producer of in the world (especially the highly sought Bourbon vanilla variety).
They are endemic to the island of Madagascar.
Lemurs have been characterized as "Madagascar's flagship mammal species" by Conservation International.
Lying off the southeastern coast of Africa, it is the world's fourth-largest island, the second-largest island country, and the 46th-largest country overall.
marojejy-bedotia.notes: The vanilla superlative, the rainforest massif and the Sava region are all quoted. I added Madagascar-page quotes to back 'huge' (fourth-largest island) and 'famous for lemurs' (flagship species). I rated it easy, not the researcher's medium, because lemurs give the country away instantly; both candidates are easy.

mafia-notho.clue: Its island lies off the coast of the country with its continent's highest mountain, facing the mangrove-lined delta of that country's longest river.
evidence: It is endemic to Mafia Island in Tanzania.
Mafia Island, (394 km2 (152 sq mi)), lies off the east coast of Tanzania opposite the delta of the Rufiji River.
It is largest and longest river in the country, formed by the confluence of the Kilombero and the Luwegu river.
The river's delta contains the largest mangrove forest in eastern Africa.

Tanzania is mountainous and densely forested in the north-east, where Mount Kilimanjaro, the highest mountain in Africa and the highest single free-standing mountain above sea level in the world, is located.
mafia-notho.notes: All quotes are present. They back the highest mountain, the longest river, the mangrove delta, and the island lying opposite that delta.

weedy-seadragon.clue: It hides in cool kelp forests on a vast reef system along a whole continent's southern coast, named after a world-famous reef further north.
evidence: It can generally be found along the entire southern coastline of the Australian continent, including Tasmania and other offshore islands.

The Great Southern Reef is a system of interconnected reefs that spans the southern coast of continental Australia and Tasmania and extends as far north as Brisbane to the east and Kalbarri to the west.
It covers 71,000 km2 (27,000 sq mi) of ocean and straddles five states, running along the coast for 8,000 km (5,000 mi).
The Great Southern Reef is named after its world-famous neighbour to the north, the Great Barrier Reef, but has received a fraction of the attention and protection given to the latter.
The robust health of the reef can be attributed to its cool, oxygen-rich waters and sprawling forests of giant and golden kelp.

The leaf-like appendages of leafy and common seadragons allow them to camouflage among the kelp and seaweeds, so well in fact that researchers started Dragon Search, a resource that allows recreational divers to report sightings of seadragons so that their population numbers may be better assessed.
All three known species of seadragon can be found only on the Great Southern Reef.
weedy-seadragon.notes: I added quotes for 'vast' (71,000 km2, 8,000 km of coast) and for common seadragons camouflaging among kelp, which the researcher's evidence did not cover. 'Named after a world-famous reef' is quoted directly.

zebra-pleco.clue: Its rapids sit on a big bend of a clear-water tributary of the world's largest river by volume, in the biggest river basin on earth.
evidence: This catfish is endemic to a small section of the Rio Xingu in Brazil. It occurs in the big bend area of the river, downstream from the town of Altamira, Para.
It is a southeast tributary of the Amazon River and one of the largest clearwater rivers in the Amazon basin, accounting for about 5% of its water.

Construction of this dam was under legal challenge by environment and indigenous groups, who assert the dam would have negative environmental and social impacts along with reducing the flow by up to 80% along a 100 km (60 mi) stretch known as the Volta Grande ("Big Bend").
The river flow in this stretch is highly complex and includes major sections of rapids.
The Amazon River in South America is the largest river in the world by discharge volume of water, and the second-longest or longest river system in the world, a title which is disputed with the Nile.
The Amazon basin, the largest in the world, covers about 40% of South America, an area of approximately 7,050,000 square kilometres (2,722,020 sq mi).
zebra-pleco.notes: Every quote is present. They back the clear-water tributary, the big bend with its rapids, the largest river by discharge and the largest basin.

red-handfish.clue: Its last reefs lie in a bay near the capital of the island state where the screeching, black-furred marsupial 'devil' now survives.
evidence: Currently, the species has been found only on two small reefs in Frederick Henry Bay.
Frederick Henry Bay is a body of water in the southeast of Tasmania, Australia.
The bay contains Seven Mile Beach on its northern shores, the closest surfing beach to Hobart.
Tasmania (/tæzˈmeɪniə/; palawa kani: Lutruwita) is an island state of Australia.
The state capital and largest city is Hobart, with around 40% of the population living in the Greater Hobart area.
It was formerly present across mainland Australia, but became extinct there around 3,500 years ago; it is now confined to the island of Tasmania.
It is characterised by its stocky and muscular build, black fur, pungent odour, extremely loud screech, keen sense of smell, and ferocity when feeding.
red-handfish.notes: I added the 'island state' quote. 'Near the capital' rests on the bay holding Hobart's closest surfing beach. The devil's black fur, loud screech and confinement to the island are quoted directly. The clue describes the fish's current two-reef range.

robertsons-wrasse.clue: Its reef rings the only coral island in the eastern part of its ocean, about 1,100 km south-west of the country where maize was first domesticated.
evidence: Thalassoma robertsoni is a species of wrasse only known to occur in the waters around Clipperton Island.
The island is the only coral island in the eastern Pacific.
Clipperton is a ring-shaped atoll that completely encloses a stagnant fresh water lagoon and measures 12 km (7.5 mi) in circumference and 720 hectares (2.8 sq mi) in area.

The coral island is located at 10°18′N 109°13′W in the East Pacific, 1,080 km (583 nmi) southwest of Mexico, 2,424 km (1,309 nmi) west of Nicaragua, 2,545 km (1,374 nmi) west of Costa Rica, and 2,390 km (1,290 nmi) northwest of the Galápagos Islands in Ecuador.
Mexico is the site of the domestication of maize, tomato, and beans, which produced an agricultural surplus.
robertsons-wrasse.notes: 'Only coral island in the eastern Pacific', the 1,080 km south-west distance and maize domestication are all quoted directly. I added the ring-shaped atoll quote for 'rings'. It doesn't overlap the angelfish clue, which uses the cliff-diver resort city and the owner country.

dageraad.clue: Its reefs stretch from a bay where penguins stroll on a town beach, near a city under a famous flat-topped mountain, east to a very busy port.
evidence: Chrysoblephus cristiceps is endemic to the southwestern Indian Ocean into the southeastern Atlantic Ocean where it has a distribution restricted to the waters off South Africa between Durban, KwaZulu-Natal and False Bay in the Western Cape.
It is located on the eastern side of the Cape Peninsula, in Simon's Town, in the southern region of Cape Town, South Africa.
Although set in a residential area, it is one of the few sites where African penguins can be observed at close range, wandering freely in a protected natural environment.

Bordered mainly by indigenous bush above the high-water mark on the one side, and the clear water of False Bay on the other, the area comprises several small sheltered bays, partially enclosed by granite boulders that are 540 million years old.
Much of the bay is off the coast of the City of Cape Town, and it includes part of the Table Mountain National Park Marine Protected Area and the whole of the Helderberg Marine Protected Area.
Afrikaans: Tafelberg) is a flat-topped mountain forming a prominent landmark overlooking the city of Cape Town in South Africa.
In November 2011, Table Mountain was named one of the New7Wonders of Nature.
Situated on the east coast of South Africa, on the Natal Bay of the Indian Ocean, Durban is the busiest port city in sub-Saharan Africa and was formerly named Port Natal.
dageraad.notes: Both ends of the range are covered: the False Bay penguin beach and the busy port of Durban. I added quotes placing Boulders Beach in a town (Simon's Town) and backing 'famous' with the New7Wonders listing.

whites-seahorse.clue: Its harbour is where its continent's first colonial settlement was founded in 1788, just up the coast from where a famous navigator landed in 1770.
evidence: White's Seahorse is locally abundant in Port Stephens and Sydney Harbour.
Population information for H. whitei is available from two estuaries in Australia: Port Stephens and Port Jackson.
Port Jackson, commonly known as Sydney Harbour, is a natural harbour on the east coast of Australia, around which the city of Sydney is situated.
As the location of the first permanent European settlement on the Australian mainland, Port Jackson has played a key role in the history of Sydney, as well as its social and economic development.
Phillip returned to Sydney Cove in HM Armed Tender Supply on 26 January 1788, where he established the first colony in Australia, later to become the city of Sydney.
Botany Bay (Dharawal: Kamay) is an open oceanic embayment, located in Sydney, New South Wales, Australia, 13 km (8 mi) south of the Sydney central business district.
On 29 April 1770, Botany Bay was the site of James Cook's first landing of His Majesty's Bark Endeavour on the land mass of Australia, after his extensive navigation of New Zealand.
whites-seahorse.notes: I confirmed the Fishes of Australia quote on the live page and added the 'Port Jackson, commonly known as Sydney Harbour' quote. The 1788 colony and the 1770 landing 13 km south are quoted directly. Botany Bay is used only as a landmark.

butterfly-splitfin.clue: Its springs lie beside a world heritage landscape of blue agave fields, the plant distilled into a famous spirit that shares its name with a nearby town.
evidence: A remnant population was found to persist in El Rincón waterpark, where the Rio Teuchitlán's springs have been dammed for bathing, between Teuchitlán town and he prehistoric site of Guachimontones, but it is unclear if this population still survives.

Situated in the hills above the town of Teuchitlán that provides the namesake for the culture that built the site, Los Guachimontones is part of the Agave Landscape and Ancient Industrial Facilities of Tequila UNESCO world heritage site and a major tourist attraction within the Tequila Valleys.
UNESCO has added the whole region, including the nearby tequila distilleries, to its World Heritage List.

The 35,019-hectare site is part of an expansive landscape of blue agave, shaped by the culture of the plant used since the 16th century to produce the spirit known as tequila and for at least two millennia to make fermented drinks (such as pulque) and cloth.
The site includes the living, working agave fields and the urban settlements of Tequila, Magdalena, El Arenal and Amatitan.

Tequila (; Spanish: [teˈkila] ) is a distilled beverage made from the blue agave plant, primarily in the area surrounding the town of Tequila 65 km (40 mi) northwest of Guadalajara, and in the Jaliscan Highlands (Los Altos de Jalisco) of the central western Mexican state of Jalisco.
A variety of cocktails are made with tequila, including the margarita, a cocktail that helped make tequila popular in the United States.
butterfly-splitfin.notes: The springs lie between Teuchitlán and Guachimontones, which is part of the agave world heritage site. I added quotes showing the site takes in the town of Tequila and the 'nearby' distilleries. The springs are the Río Teuchitlán type locality, inside the input range.

nassau-grouper.clue: Its reefs run from a famous 'triangle' where ships are said to vanish, south through warm island seas where pirates once hunted treasure fleets.
evidence: It lives in the western Atlantic Ocean and around the Caribbean Sea, from Bermuda, Florida, and the Bahamas in the north to the eastern coast of Venezuela, but it is only found in a few places in the Gulf of Mexico, most notably along the coast of Belize.
The Nassau grouper lives near reefs; it is one of the largest fish to be found around coral reefs.
The Bermuda Triangle, also known as the Devil's Triangle, is a loosely defined region in the North Atlantic Ocean, roughly bounded by Florida, Bermuda, and Puerto Rico.
Since the mid-20th century, it has been the focus of an urban legend suggesting that many aircraft, ships, and people have disappeared there under mysterious circumstances.
The Caribbean Sea is a sea of the North Atlantic Ocean in the tropics of the Western Hemisphere, located south of the Gulf of Mexico and southwest of the Sargasso Sea.

It is bounded by the Greater Antilles to the north from Cuba to Puerto Rico, the Lesser Antilles to the east from the Virgin Islands to Trinidad and Tobago, South America to the south from the Venezuelan coastline to the Colombian coastline, and Central America and the Yucatán Peninsula to the west from Panama to Mexico.
In the 16th century, pirate captains recruited seamen to loot European merchant ships, especially the Spanish treasure fleets sailing from the Caribbean to Europe.
nassau-grouper.notes: Nothing the researcher cited supported 'warm island seas', so I fetched the Caribbean Sea page (a tropical sea bounded by island chains) and added the grouper's reef habitat. The triangle legend and the pirates' treasure fleets are quoted directly.

brazilian-guitarfish.clue: Its waters stretch south from a city famed for carnival and a mountaintop statue, down to the wide estuary where tango was born.
evidence: Western South Atlantic: From Rio de Janeiro to Argentina.

Rio de Janeiro is one of the most visited cities in the Southern Hemisphere and is known for its natural settings, carnival, samba, bossa nova, and beaches such as Barra da Tijuca, Copacabana, Ipanema, and Leblon.
the statue of Christ the Redeemer atop Corcovado mountain
originated in the 1880s along the Río de la Plata, the natural border between Argentina and Uruguay.
The Río de la Plata behaves as an estuary in which freshwater and seawater mix.
If considered a river, it is the widest in the world, with a maximum width of 220 kilometres (140 mi).
brazilian-guitarfish.notes: Changed 'down past the wide estuary' to 'down to the wide estuary': FishBase gives the range only as 'From Rio de Janeiro to Argentina', which does not show it extends beyond the estuary. Carnival, the Corcovado statue, tango's origin and the estuary's width all confirmed on the cited pages.

licorice-gourami.clue: Its island has been mined for tin for about 300 years. It lies just east of a huge island, crossed by the equator, that is home to tigers and orangutans.
evidence: It is endemic to Bangka in Indonesia where it is found in the slow, flowing streams with black waters
Soon after, around 1710, tin was discovered on the island which attracted migrants from across the archipelago and beyond.
Since circa 1710, Bangka has been one of the world's main tin-producing centers.
It lies just east of Sumatra, separated by the Bangka Strait;
the equator crossing the island at its centre
the sixth-largest island in the world at 482,286.55 km2
Species found in Sumatra now critically endangered include the Sumatran tiger, Sumatran elephant, Sumatran rhinoceros, Sumatran orangutan and Tapanuli orangutan.
licorice-gourami.notes: Tin since about 1710 (about 316 years), 'just east of Sumatra', the equator, the island's size (sixth-largest) and its tigers and orangutans are all confirmed on the cited pages. The fish is endemic to Bangka.

kutubu-rainbowfish.clue: Its mountain lake lies in the world's most language-rich country, with about 840 languages, on the island that is the world centre of birds-of-paradise.
evidence: It is one of 13 fish endemic to Lake Kutubu, a lake found within the Kikori River system in Papua New Guinea.
It is one of the few lakes in the country that occurs in a depression in the rugged interior mountains.
There are 840 known spoken languages, making it the most linguistically diverse country in the world.
is an island nation in Oceania that comprises the eastern half of the island of New Guinea
The centre of bird-of-paradise diversity is the large island of New Guinea
kutubu-rainbowfish.notes: The mountain setting, the 840 languages and 'most linguistically diverse', and New Guinea as the centre of bird-of-paradise diversity are all confirmed. Endemic range matches.

kaluga.clue: Its river forms part of the border between two giant countries and shares its name with a rare tiger that prowls the forests nearby.
evidence: found in the Amur River basin from Russia to China and near Hokkaido in Japan.
for part of its length forms the border between China and Russia
It flows east forming the border between China and Russia
It is the largest country in the world, spanning eleven time zones and sharing land borders with fourteen countries.
Covering 9.6 million square kilometers (3,700,000 sq mi), it is the third largest country by area.
The Siberian tiger or Amur tiger is a population of the tiger subspecies
Felis tigris var. amurensis proposed by Charles Dode in 1871 was based on tiger skins from the Amur region.
Other animals inhabiting this region include the Amur falcon, Amur leopard and Amur tiger
As of 2022, about 756 Siberian tigers, including 200 cubs, were estimated to inhabit the Russian Far East.
Key habitats of the Siberian tiger are Korean pine forests with a complex composition and structure.
kaluga.notes: Changed 'forms a long border' to 'forms part of the border': no cited page gives the border length, and the kaluga page says 'for part of its length'. Added the Russia and China pages to back 'giant countries' (largest and third-largest by area). The Amur tiger name, its rarity and its forest habitat are confirmed.

binni.clue: Its marshes lie between two famous rivers, in the ancient land credited with the wheel, early writing and some of the world's earliest civilisations.
evidence: The marshes are primarily located on the floodplains of the Euphrates and Tigris rivers
As its name suggests, the Mesopotamian Marshes are located in the larger region of Mesopotamia.
Mesopotamia encompasses the land between the Euphrates and Tigris rivers
inspired some of the most important developments in human history, including the invention of the wheel
It is recognised as the cradle of some of the world's earliest civilizations.
The region was home to one of the four riverine civilizations where writing was invented
binni.notes: The marshes between the Tigris and Euphrates, the wheel, the invention of writing and 'cradle of some of the world's earliest civilizations' are all confirmed. This is the fish's core range in southern Iraq. It is on the easy side of medium.

gulf-grouper.clue: A famous ocean explorer called its sea 'the aquarium of the world'. The sea splits a long desert peninsula from its country's mainland.
evidence: It is found throughout the Gulf of California and around the Revillagigedos Islands.
Dazzled by its unmatched natural beauty, Cousteau famously dubbed the Sea of Cortez the 'aquarium of the world'.
When Jacques Cousteau embarked on an epic mission to the Sea of Cortez in 1987...
was a French naval officer, oceanographer, filmmaker and author.
a marginal sea of the Pacific Ocean that separates the Baja California peninsula from the Mexican mainland.
The climate of Baja California peninsula is predominantly a hot desert climate
With a length of 1,247 km (775 miles)
gulf-grouper.notes: The Cousteau quote is on the cited page. I added the Cousteau page to back 'ocean explorer' (oceanographer) and the peninsula's length for 'long'. The clue targets the Gulf of California core; the San Diego records were vagrants.

humpback-chub.clue: Its canyon river, named for its reddish silt, waters 40 million people and is used so heavily it has rarely reached the sea since the 1960s.
evidence: species persists only in turbulent, high-gradient, canyon-bound reaches
The name Colorado derives from the Spanish language for "colored reddish" due to its heavy silt load.
a vital source of water for 40 million people
rarely reached the sea since the 1960s
humpback-chub.notes: The reddish-silt name, the 40 million people (river plus tributaries) and the river rarely reaching the sea since the 1960s are all confirmed on the cited pages. The fish lives in canyon reaches of this river system.

angelshark.clue: Its stronghold today is a volcanic island chain off the coast of the world's largest hot desert, home to the highest peak of the country that owns it.
evidence: Secure the future of the Critically Endangered Angelshark in its unique stronghold of the Canary Islands
Raise awareness that the Canary Islands is the unique Angelshark stronghold in Europe.
Healthy subpopulations of angelsharks are thought to still persist in areas off North Africa and around the Canary Islands,
about 100 kilometres (60 mi) off the northwest coast of Africa
all of which are volcanic in origin
Mount Teide is the highest peak in Spain
The Sahara is the world's largest hot desert.
It stretches from the Red Sea in the east and the Mediterranean in the north to the Atlantic Ocean in the west
angelshark.notes: Changed 'Its last stronghold is' to 'Its stronghold today is': Wikipedia says healthy subpopulations may also persist off North Africa, so 'last' overstates. The volcanic islands, Mount Teide as Spain's highest peak and the Sahara reaching the Atlantic are confirmed.

tawilis.clue: Its lake lies about 50 km south of its country's capital, in a nation of over 7,000 islands named after a 16th-century king.
evidence: S. tawilis populations are only found in Taal Lake in the Batangas province on the island of Luzon in the Philippines.
Located in the province of Batangas about 50 kilometers (31 mi) south of Manila
Manila is the country's capital
consists of about 7,641 islands, with a total area of about 300,000 square kilometers.
named the archipelago las Islas Filipinas in honor of King Philip II.
21 May 1527 – 13 September 1598
the Philippines, named in his honour by Ruy López de Villalobos.
tawilis.notes: The 50 km is the distance from Manila to Taal Volcano, whose island sits near the middle of the lake, so it holds for the lake too. I added the Philip II page to confirm he was a 16th-century king (reigned from 1556, died 1598).

spring-pygmy-sunfish.clue: Its springs are in a southern state nicknamed for cotton, where a famous bus boycott and protest marches made civil-rights history.
evidence: The spring pygmy sunfish, Elassoma alabamae, is a species of pygmy sunfish endemic to springs in northern Alabama.
Alabama is also known as the "Heart of Dixie" and the "Cotton State".
The civil rights movement had notable events in Alabama, including the Montgomery bus boycott
spring-pygmy-sunfish.notes: The Cotton State nickname and the bus boycott are confirmed, and the same page lists the 1965 Selma to Montgomery marches. The fish is endemic to springs in northern Alabama.

powder-blue-panchax.clue: Its mainland river runs down from its island nation's highest peak, through the country's main cocoa valley and forests with their own woolly lemur.
evidence: endemic to Madagascar where it is found on the island of Nosy Be and in the Sambirano River basin
It has its sources at the Maromokotra peak and flows through the Tsaratanana Reserve to the Indian Ocean.
The highest point is Maromokotro, in the Tsaratanana Massif region in the north of the island, at 2,876 metres (9,436 ft).
The valley of the Sambirano is the main cocoa producing area of Madagascar.
has many indigenous species, such as the Sambirano mouse lemur and Sambirano woolly lemur.
powder-blue-panchax.notes: The source peak (spelled Maromokotra on one page and Maromokotro on the other, the same summit) is the country's highest point. The main cocoa valley and the Sambirano woolly lemur are confirmed. The fish lives in the Sambirano basin.

myaka.clue: It lives in a crater lake on the same chain of volcanoes as a lake that burst out a huge cloud of carbon dioxide in 1986.
evidence: endemic to Lake Barombi Mbo in western Cameroon.
It is located in the Cameroon volcanic chain, and is the largest volcanic lake in this region.
Volcanism here has created crater lakes.
On 21 August 1986, one of these, Lake Nyos, belched carbon dioxide and killed between 1,700 and 2,000 people.
The mountain is part of the area of volcanic activity known as the Cameroon Volcanic Line
which also includes Lake Nyos, the site of a disaster in 1986
myaka.notes: Changed 'killing over 1,700 people' to 'killing at least 1,700 people' to match the source's 'between 1,700 and 2,000'. The clue is about Lake Nyos, not the fish's own lake, so it does not repeat the revealFact's gas-risk line, although the theme is related. Lead edit: dropped the death toll to keep clues cheerful; the 1986 carbon dioxide release is still supported by the cited evidence.

dalmatian-barbelgudgeon.clue: It lives in the coastal region that gave its name to a spotted dog breed once trained to run in front of horse-drawn fire carriages.
evidence: It is found in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, where it inhabits the karst.
It occurs in some creeks in the Livanjsko field, in the Cetina, Krka and perhaps Zrmanja Rivers
a river in Croatia's Dalmatia region, known for its numerous waterfalls.
an eastern Adriatic coastal belt with a Mediterranean climate
The Dalmatian is a breed of dog with a white coat marked with dark-coloured spots.
it was also used as a carriage dog by firefighters in the days of horse-drawn firehouse carriages.
the dogs were easily trained to run in front of the carriages to help clear a path
The origins of this breed can be traced to Croatia and the historical region of Dalmatia.
dalmatian-barbelgudgeon.notes: Removed 'sunny' (no source mentions sunshine) and changed 'used to run beside' to 'trained to run in front of', which is what the dog page says. The coastal region, spotted breed, firefighter carriage use and Dalmatian origin are confirmed. The echo of the fish's name is allowed.

beluga.clue: Its main home is the world's largest lake, a slightly salty inland sea, and it swims up the longest river on its continent to spawn.
evidence: It is found primarily in the Caspian and Black Sea basins, and formerly in the Adriatic Sea.
The Caspian Sea is the world's largest inland body of water,
also described as the world's largest lake and usually referred to as a full-fledged sea.
It has a salinity of approximately 1.2% (12 g/L)
Its main freshwater inflow, Europe's longest river, the Volga, enters at the shallow north end.
This river historically held most of the world's beluga spawners and releases
In its major spawning river the Volga, only a small percentage (less than 20%) of beluga are able to migrate upstream…
beluga.notes: The 'largest lake', the 1.2% salinity and the Volga as Europe's longest river are confirmed. The Animal Diversity Web page names the Volga as its major spawning river with most of the world's spawners, which supports 'main home'.

humpbacked-limia.clue: Its lake is in the only country in history founded through a successful slave revolt, which declared independence in 1804.
evidence: Limia nigrofasciata exclusively inhabits Lake Miragoâne, but it is not particular about the type of substrate.
Lake Miragoâne (French: Étang de Miragoâne) is a lake in Haiti, located one kilometer southeast of the city of Miragoâne.
the only country in history established by a slave revolt.
On 1 January 1804, the leaders of the Haitian Revolution declared their achieved independence from France.
humpbacked-limia.notes: 'The only country in history established by a slave revolt' and the 1 January 1804 independence date are confirmed on the Haiti page. The lake is the fish's only habitat.

damba-mipentina.clue: One of its rivers drains the highland capital of a huge island nation, then feeds a river flowing down through ever drier country to mangroves on the north-west coast.
evidence: The damba mipentina (Paretroplus maculatus) is a critically endangered species of cichlid fish from turbid, shallow flood-plain lakes in the Betsiboka and Ikopa River basins in northwestern Madagascar.
The Betsiboka's largest tributary, the Ikopa River, drains the capital city of Antananarivo.
It flows northwestward and empties to Bombetoka Bay, forming a large delta.
The Betsiboka is surrounded in mangroves, and is distinctive for its red-coloured water, which is caused by river sediments.
Its spring, named Varahina, is found in the sub-prefecture of Andramasina at an altitude of 1810 meters.
Lying off the southeastern coast of Africa, it is the world's fourth-largest island, the second-largest island country, and the 46th-largest country overall.
Antananarivo, the administrative capital and largest city of Madagascar, is located in the highlands region, near the island's geographic center.
To the west of the highlands, the increasingly arid terrain gradually slopes down to the Mozambique Channel and mangrove swamps along the coast.
damba-mipentina.notes: Changed 'then winds down through ever drier country to mangroves' to 'then feeds a river flowing down through ever drier country to mangroves'. The capital's river (Ikopa) is a tributary, and only the Betsiboka it feeds reaches the mangrove coast. I added the fourth-largest-island quote to back 'huge'.

banggai-cardinalfish.clue: Its islands belong to the world's largest island nation, just off the eastern arm of a contorted island with four peninsulas.
evidence: This species is restricted to the Banggai Islands of Indonesia.
The Banggai cardinalfish is composed of isolated populations concentrated around the shallows of 17 large and 10 small islands within the Banggai Archipelago.
Peleng, off the East Peninsula of Sulawesi
Peleng is an island off the east coast of Sulawesi, Indonesia and is the largest island of the Banggai Islands (Kepulauan Banggai).
The landmass of Sulawesi includes four peninsulas: the northern Minahasa Peninsula, the East Peninsula, the South Peninsula, and the Southeast Peninsula.

The first Europeans to visit the island (which they believed to be an archipelago due to its contorted shape) were the Portuguese sailors Simão de Abreu in 1523, and Gomes de Sequeira (among others) in 1525, sent from the Moluccas in search of gold, which the islands had the reputation of producing.
Comprising between 13,000 and 17,000 islands—including Sumatra, Java, Sulawesi, and parts of Borneo and New Guinea—it is the world's largest archipelagic state and the 14th-largest country by area.
banggai-cardinalfish.notes: I removed 'small' from 'Its small islands', because the fish lives around 17 large and 10 small islands and Peleng covers about 2,489 km². I also removed 'long' from 'four long peninsulas', because the source only says 'four peninsulas'. I read 'island nation' as plain wording for 'archipelagic state'.

blind-swamp-eel.clue: Its flooded sinkholes pit a limestone peninsula that sits right on top of the buried crater from the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs.
evidence: The blind swamp eel is endemic to the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico where it inhabits freshwater in sinkholes and limestone caves.
The Chicxulub crater is an impact crater buried underneath the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico.
It was formed slightly over 66 million years ago when an asteroid, about ten kilometers (six miles) in diameter, struck Earth.

It is now widely accepted that the devastation and climate disruption resulting from the impact was the primary cause of the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event, a mass extinction of 75% of plant and animal species on Earth, including all non-avian dinosaurs.

A cenote (English: /sɪ.ˈnoʊ.ti/ or /sɛ.ˈnoʊ.teɪ/, sih-NO-tee or seh-NO-tay; Latin American Spanish: [seˈnote]) is a natural pit, or sinkhole, resulting when a collapse of limestone bedrock exposes groundwater.
Although cenotes are found widely throughout much of the Yucatán Peninsula, a higher-density circular alignment of cenotes overlies the measured rim of the Chicxulub crater.
blind-swamp-eel.notes: I removed 'flat' from 'a flat limestone peninsula', because none of the cited pages describe the peninsula as flat. 'Limestone' is backed by the eel and cenote pages, the asteroid by the crater page, and 'the dinosaurs' means the non-avian dinosaurs that source names.

devils-hole-pupfish.clue: Its warm desert pool is a detached outpost of the hottest, driest and lowest national park in its country.
evidence: Devils Hole is a geologic formation located in a detached unit of Death Valley National Park and surrounded by the Ash Meadows National Wildlife Refuge, in Nye County, Nevada, in the Southwestern United States.
Devils Hole is habitat for the only naturally occurring population of the endangered Devils Hole pupfish (Cyprinodon diabolis).
Devils Hole is a geothermal pool within a limestone cavern in the Amargosa Desert in the Amargosa Valley of Nevada, east over the Amargosa Range and Funeral Mountains from Death Valley.
It is at an elevation of 730 m (2,400 ft) above sea level and the water is a constant temperature of 33 °C (91 °F).
Death Valley is the largest national park in the contiguous United States, as well as the hottest, driest and lowest of all the national parks in the United States.
devils-hole-pupfish.notes: Every claim checks out: 'warm' is the constant 33 °C, 'desert pool' is the geothermal pool in the Amargosa Desert, 'detached outpost' is the detached unit, and the superlatives are quoted word for word. It does not repeat the funFact or revealFact.

hong-kong-grouper.clue: Scientists first described it from a harbour city whose tiny artificial island was its country's only door to western traders for over 200 years.
evidence: It is found in southern Japan where it occurs in the Tsugaru Strait, the strait between Honshu and Hokkaido south along both coasts.

The Hong Kong grouper was first formally described as Serranus akaara in 1842 by the Dutch zoologist Coenraad Jacob Temminck (1778-1858) and his student, the German ichthyologist Hermann Schlegel (1804-1884), with the type locality given as Nagasaki.

Dejima (Japanese: 出島; lit. 'exit island') or Deshima, in the 17th century also called Tsukishima (築島; lit. 'built island'), was an artificial island off Nagasaki, Japan, that served as a trading post for the Portuguese (1570–1639) and subsequently the Dutch (1641–1858).
For 220 years, it was the central conduit for foreign trade and cultural exchange with Japan during the isolationist Edo period (1600–1869), and the only Japanese territory open to Westerners.
Dejima was a small island, 120 meters (390 ft) by 75 m (246 ft), linked to the mainland by a small bridge, guarded on both sides, and with a gate on the Dutch side.
In 1570 daimyō Ōmura Sumitada converted to Catholicism (choosing Bartolomeu as his Christian name) and made a deal with the Portuguese to develop Nagasaki; soon the port was open for trade.
hong-kong-grouper.notes: The type locality, Nagasaki, sits inside the native range in southern Japan. 'Tiny' is backed by the 120 m by 75 m figure, 'harbour city' by Nagasaki's port, and '200+ years as the only door' by the 220 years. I rated it medium rather than hard, because Japan's long isolation with a single western trading post is general-knowledge history.

west-african-seahorse.clue: Its warm coastal waters curve around the gulf where the equator crosses the prime meridian, on the west coast of a vast continent.
evidence: It is found in the eastern central Atlantic Ocean off Angola, Benin, Ivory Coast, Gambia, Ghana, Guinea, Liberia, Nigeria, São Tomé and Príncipe, Senegal, and Sierra Leone, as well as the Canary Islands.

The Gulf of Guinea (French: Golfe de Guinée; Spanish: Golfo de Guinea; Portuguese: Golfo da Guiné) is the northeasternmost part of the tropical Atlantic Ocean from Cape Lopez in Gabon, north and west to Cape Palmas in Liberia.
Null Island, defined as the intersection of the Equator and Prime Meridian (zero degrees latitude and longitude), is in the gulf.
west-african-seahorse.notes: The gulf-coast countries (Ivory Coast, Ghana, Benin, Nigeria, São Tomé) are all in the native list, 'warm' rests on 'tropical Atlantic', and Null Island is quoted directly. The clue does not lean on the recent Canary Islands records.

delta-smelt.clue: Its brackish waters drain through a chain of bays, then out to sea under what a travel guide calls the world's most photographed bridge.
evidence: The delta smelt is endemic to the Sacramento–San Joaquin River Delta in California, where it is distributed from the Suisun Bay upstream through the delta in Contra Costa, Sacramento, San Joaquin, and Solano Counties.
They are euryhaline but occur mostly at salinities of 0–7 practical salinity units.

Water from the Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers, and from the Sierra Nevada mountains, flow into Suisun Bay, which then travels through the Carquinez Strait to meet with the Napa River at the entrance to San Pablo Bay, which connects at its south end to San Francisco Bay.
It then connects to the Pacific Ocean via the Golden Gate strait.
The Golden Gate Bridge is a suspension bridge spanning the Golden Gate, the one-mile-wide (1.6 km) strait connecting San Francisco Bay and the Pacific Ocean in California, United States.
The Golden Gate Bridge is described in Frommer's travel guide as "possibly the most beautiful, certainly the most photographed, bridge in the world".
delta-smelt.notes: I removed 'west' from 'drain west through a chain of bays', because no cited source states the direction. The chain of bays, the bridge over the outlet strait, and the Frommer's 'most photographed' quote all check out.

splendid-toadfish.clue: It lurks on the second-largest barrier reef in the world, which begins at the tip of a limestone peninsula pocked with thousands of sinkholes.
evidence: The splendid toadfish (Sanopus splendidus) also called the coral toadfish and the Cozumel splendid toadfish is a species of toadfish once believed to be entirely endemic to the island of Cozumel but have been found on the reefs of Honduras all the way up to Cancun.

It begins near Isla Contoy on the northern tip of the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico and continues south alongside the entire Riviera Maya, including areas like Cancún, Playa del Carmen, Tulum, Cozumel, and on to the southernmost point of coastal Quintana Roo, with Banco Chinchorro and Xcalak.
It is the largest barrier reef in the Western Hemisphere.
It is the second largest after the Great Barrier Reef of Australia; the MBRS is much less researched and recognized.

A cenote (English: /sɪ.ˈnoʊ.ti/ or /sɛ.ˈnoʊ.teɪ/, sih-NO-tee or seh-NO-tay; Latin American Spanish: [seˈnote]) is a natural pit, or sinkhole, resulting when a collapse of limestone bedrock exposes groundwater.
The Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico alone has an estimated 10,000 cenotes.
splendid-toadfish.notes: 'Second-largest barrier reef' comes from the reef-system page (largest barrier reef in the Western Hemisphere, second only to the Great Barrier Reef), and 'thousands of sinkholes' is the estimated 10,000 cenotes. The fish's range, Honduras to Cancún, lies along this reef.

red-steenbras.clue: Its reefs run from a bay beneath a flat-topped mountain, round the southern tip of its continent, to a wetland of hippos and crocodiles.
evidence: The red steenbras is endemic to South Africa where it occurs from Table Bay in the Western Cape to St Lucia, KwaZulu-Natal.
It is found at depths between 5 and 150 m (16 and 492 ft), with the adults found on offshore rocky reefs at depths greater than 50 m (160 ft) while the juveniles are found in shallower reefs.
Overlooked by Cape Town, the bay is dominated by the flat-topped Table Mountain, from which it takes its name.

It is both the southernmost point of South Africa, the geographic southern tip of Africa and the beginning of the traditional dividing line between the Atlantic and Indian oceans according to the International Hydrographic Organization.

It is South Africa's third-largest protected area, spanning 280 km (170 mi) of coastline, from the Mozambican border in the north to Mapelane south of the Lake St. Lucia estuary, and made up of around 3,280 km2 (1,270 sq mi) of natural ecosystems, managed by the iSimangaliso Authority.
The park was previously known as the Greater St. Lucia Wetland Park, but was renamed on 1 November 2007.
The park is also home to 1,200 crocodiles and 800 hippopotami.
red-steenbras.notes: I removed 'famous' from 'a famous flat-topped mountain', because the Table Bay page only calls the mountain flat-topped. The range from Table Bay to St Lucia necessarily rounds the continent's southern tip and ends in the hippo and crocodile wetland park.

california-golden-trout.clue: Its creeks share a county and a mountain range with the biggest known living tree in the world, measured by volume.
evidence: The golden trout is commonly found at elevations from 6,890 feet (2,100 m) to 10,000 feet (3,000 m) above sea level, and is native to California's southern Sierra Nevada mountains.
Golden Trout Creek is an approximately 9-mile (14 km) long tributary of the Kern River, flowing in northeastern Tulare County, California.
The General Sherman Tree is a giant sequoia (Sequoiadendron giganteum) tree in the Giant Forest of Sequoia National Park in Tulare County, California.
By volume, it is the largest known living single-stem tree on Earth.

Notable features include the General Sherman Tree, the largest tree in the world by volume; Lake Tahoe, the largest alpine lake in North America; Mount Whitney at 14,505 ft (4,421 m), the highest point in the contiguous United States; and Yosemite Valley sculpted by glaciers from one-hundred-million-year-old granite, containing high waterfalls.
